title: npm 12 Released: Install Scripts Off by Default as Registry Moves to Explicit Trust
gist: npm 12 flips lifecycle install scripts, Git dependencies and remote tarballs to deny-by-default, closing vectors JFrog links to roughly 53% of malicious npm attacks in the past year; npm is the last major JavaScript package manager to adopt controls pnpm, yarn and bun already shipped, and researchers warn approval fatigue could turn the allowlist into a click-through prompt.

insights.claim: npm 12 sets allowScripts to off by default, so dependency preinstall, install and postinstall scripts no longer run unless explicitly allowlisted in package.json, including implicit node-gyp builds triggered by any package containing a binding.gyp file even with no declared install script.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: The largest software registry moving to explicit trust is a structural change to JavaScript supply-chain risk; expect broken CI across the ecosystem on upgrade.
insights.quote: The headline change is that allowScripts now defaults to off.

insights.claim: npm 12 sets --allow-git to none, closing a code-execution path in which a Git dependency's own .npmrc could override the Git executable even when --ignore-scripts was set, and sets --allow-remote to none to block https tarball dependencies, while --allow-file and --allow-directory are unchanged.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: The .npmrc-overrides-Git-binary path shows --ignore-scripts was never a complete mitigation — security teams relying on it should re-audit.
insights.locator: The other two defaults target non registry sources

insights.claim: The npm 12 defaults were announced in June and shipped behind warnings from npm 11.16.0, giving teams a preparation window before the hard cutover.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Staged warning periods are how registry maintainers de-risk ecosystem-wide breaking changes — a template for other package managers.
insights.locator: The changes were first announced in June

insights.claim: GitHub's migration guidance is to allow what is already in the dependency tree first and then tighten, with documented recipes for native modules, Cypress, Playwright, Puppeteer, Electron and Husky.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: The named packages are the practical blast radius — any toolchain using them needs an allowlist change before upgrading.

insights.claim: Global installs and npx cannot use npm approve-scripts and must be configured via config instead, for example npm config set allow-scripts=canvas,sharp --location=user.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: A gap in the ergonomics that will drive users toward blanket user-level allowlists, weakening the control.
insights.locator: Global installs and npx cannot use approve-scripts

insights.claim: An existing ignore-scripts=true setting takes precedence and silently defeats the new allowlist, and npm approve-scripts reads from node_modules so it errors with ENOMATCH for packages not yet installed — a chicken-and-egg problem for new dependencies.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Silent precedence failures produce false confidence in a security control; verify effective config rather than assuming the default holds.
insights.quote: an existing ignore-scripts=true takes precedence and silently defeats the allowlist

themes.theme: Approval fatigue as the residual risk

insights.claim: Security researchers argue approval fatigue is the bigger risk than the scripts themselves, because widely used packages like esbuild, sharp, core-js, puppeteer and bcrypt all rely on lifecycle scripts, so repeated broken builds will degrade deny-by-default into a click-through prompt.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: The control's real efficacy depends on how many legitimate packages need approval — watch whether ecosystem maintainers remove lifecycle scripts, not just whether npm ships the default.
insights.quote: repeated broken builds will turn deny by default into ‘a click-through prompt’, while pushing attacker activity onto surfaces with less visibility
insights.locator: Security researchers have raised approval fatigue

insights.claim: JFrog reports the three install vectors npm 12 disables were involved in roughly 53% of malicious npm attacks observed in the past year.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Quantifies the upside: roughly half of observed attack paths closed by default, with the remainder migrating to lower-visibility surfaces.
insights.quote: JFrog reports the three vectors were involved in roughly 53% of malicious npm attacks observed in the past year.

insights.claim: Community reaction skewed supportive, with the Hacker News thread drawing 484 points and more than 200 comments, though dissenters cited legitimate uses like patch-package and argued the allowlist 'has no scope' for transitive dependencies.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Broad developer buy-in lowers the odds of the default being reverted under pressure.
insights.quote: postinstall scripts should've been removed long time ago, it's the cancer of NPM packages.
insights.locator: Community reaction has been broadly supportive

insights.claim: npm is the last major package manager to adopt install-script allowlisting, which pnpm has offered for years, and it also trailed on install cooldowns: pnpm shipped minimumReleaseAge in 10.16, yarn added npmMinimalAgeGate in 4.10.0 and bun followed in 1.3 before npm's own min-release-age in 11.10.0.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: The incumbent registry client follows rather than sets the security frontier — alternative package managers remain the leading indicator for where npm defaults go next.
insights.quote: npm is also the last major package manager to adopt these controls.
insights.locator: npm is also the last major package manager

insights.claim: npm 12 also deprecates granular access tokens that bypass two-factor authentication, tightening publish-side identity alongside the install-side changes.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Publish-token hardening plus install hardening closes both ends of the account-takeover-to-victim chain that drove recent registry incidents.
insights.locator: npm, the package manager maintained by GitHub
